Robert Guibé (1460-1513) was a French Roman Catholic bishop and cardinal who played a significant role in the governance of Western Europe during the late medieval period. Born in Vitré, France, Guibé rose through the ranks of the Catholic Church to become a prominent figure in the papal court of Pope Julius II.

Guibé's influence extended beyond his ecclesiastical position, as he was also involved in the political and economic affairs of Western Europe. He participated in several diplomatic missions, including one to France in 1506, where he negotiated a treaty with King Louis XII. Additionally, Guibé was appointed as the Archbishop of Reims, a position that gave him significant authority over the region.

Despite his influential role, Guibé's legacy is not as well-documented as some of his contemporaries. However, his contributions to the Catholic Church and Western European politics are undeniable.

The 'Illuminated Hours' manuscript created during Guibé's papacy remains a testament to his artistic and cultural tastes.

Guibé's tenure also saw the rise of the Renaissance humanist movement, which emphasized classical learning and individualism. This shift in intellectual focus had far-reaching consequences for Western European culture and society.
